keywords.name: Marcus Deufert
paragraphs: German classical philologist (born 1970), professor at the University of Leipzig.
Editor of the 2019 Bibliotheca Teubneriana edition of Lucretius, currently the most authoritative critical text.
His edition features a selective but rigorous apparatus, aiming to reconstruct the archetype with minimal conjectural intervention.

keywords.name: Karl Lachmann
paragraphs: German classical and Germanic philologist (1793–1851); established the landmark stemmatic edition and demonstrated the existence and structure of archetype Ω.
Major critical edition: Titi Lucreti Cari de rerum natura libri sex. Carolus Lachmannus recensuit et emendavit, Berolini 1850.
Lachmann’s methodological principles still underpin contemporary Lucretian scholarship.

keywords.name: Sebastiano Timpanaro
paragraphs: Italian classical philologist and textual critic (1923–2000); renowned scholar of classical reception and Latin textual transmission.
Author of influential studies on the transmission of Latin texts and on Lucretius’ manuscript tradition.

keywords.name: Richard Bentley
paragraphs: English classical scholar and pioneering textual critic (1662–1742); composed celebrated marginalia and acute conjectures on the text of Lucretius.
Many of his emendations continue to appear in modern apparatuses as significant alternatives.

keywords.name: Gilbert Wakefield
paragraphs: English classical scholar and critic (1756–1801); editor of the celebrated edition Titi Lucretii Cari de rerum natura libros sex … longe emendatiores reddidit … Gilbertus Wakefield, published in London in three volumes (1796–1797).

In Deufert’s apparatus, Wakefield is cited alongside Munro, Müller, and Flores as an authoritative prior editor from whom readings and conjectures preserved in secondary Italian codices (codices Italici) are reported whenever not collated directly by Deufert himself.
His work represents a fundamental bridge between humanistic editorial traditions and early modern textual criticism.

keywords.name: Johann Caspar von Orelli
paragraphs: Swiss classical scholar and epigraphist (1787–1849); editor of Latin classical texts and philosophical anthologies.
Cited for his school anthology of Latin poetry: Eclogae poetarum latinorum in usum gymnasiorum. Edidit Io. Casparus Orellius … Turici 1822.
Although not a primary editor of the entire poem, his conjectures and lexical notes are cited in modern apparatuses.

keywords.name: Giovanni Pontano
paragraphs: Italian humanist, poet, and statesman (1426–1503), leading figure of Neapolitan humanism and head of the Accademia Pontaniana.

His emendations to Lucretius were not published in an independent edition, but survive as manuscript notes entered into two copies of the 1495 Venice edition (now in Munich and London), transcribed respectively by Petrus Victorius and Hieronymus Borgius.

In Deufert’s edition, the siglum Pont. designates conjectures shared by both copies; at III.28, his emendation ibi is adopted to heal the metrically and syntactically clumsy reading ubi transmitted by the archetype Ω.

keywords.name: Michele Marullo Tarcaniota
paragraphs: Greek-Italian Renaissance poet and humanist scholar (ca. 1458–1500). Younger than Pontano, he was intimately familiar with Pontano’s critical attempts and advanced them substantially, achieving far more in the emendation of the text.

The purest source for his conjectures is a second Munich copy of the 1495 Venice edition (Bayer. Staatsbibliothek 4° A lat a 317), which Petrus Victorius collated directly with Marullo's working book. Conjectures uniquely surviving here are designated with the siglum Mar.

In Deufert's apparatus, the siglum Mar.* designates conjectures where at least two witnesses among D², I², Ea, Fa, Da, and the 1512 Giuntina edition by Petrus Candidus agree, since Candidus explicitly followed Marullo’s recension ('Marulli censuram potissimum').

keywords.name: Richard J. Shackle
paragraphs: British classical scholar (active early 20th century); author of conjectural emendations to classical Latin poets, including Lucretius (1921).
His work reflects the renewed interest in textual emendation during the early 1900s.

keywords.name: Dionysius Lambinus
paragraphs: French Renaissance humanist and classical scholar (1516–1572), professor of Greek and Latin at the Collège Royal in Paris.

Editor of the seminal Paris edition Titi Lucretii Cari de rerum natura libri sex. A Dionysio Lambino … emendati (1563/1564), accompanied by extensive commentaries and sharp conjectural emendations based on manuscript collations.
Cited in Deufert's critical apparatus for reporting the variant eiiciuntur at III.58 and proposing the verbal conjecture uidentur at III.66.

keywords.name: Richard Heinze
paragraphs: German classical philologist (1867–1929), professor at the University of Leipzig and renowned commentator on Latin poetry and rhetoric.
Author of the influential commentary on Book III: T. Lucretius Carus. De rerum natura Buch III. Erklärt von Richard Heinze (Lipsiae 1897), providing penetrating philosophical and textual analysis.
Cited in the apparatus at III.58 for his tentative conjecture mala re proposed in his commentary notes.

keywords.name: Willy Morel
paragraphs: German classical scholar and textual critic (1894–1973), prominent editor of early Latin poetic fragments.
Contributed textual studies on Lucretian corruptions in his article Zu Lukrez (Philologus 85, 1930, 227 sq.).
Cited by Deufert in the apparatus at III.58 for the conjectural reading minaci.

keywords.name: Hugh Andrew Johnstone Munro
paragraphs: British classical scholar (1819–1885), Fellow of Trinity College and first Kennedy Professor of Latin at the University of Cambridge.

Editor of the fundamental edition, commentary and prose translation T. Lucreti Cari de rerum natura libri sex (Cambridge 1864; third edition 1873, cited in the apparatus as Munro³), which dominated Anglophone Lucretian scholarship for decades.
Cited by Deufert at III.82: he posited a lacuna after this line and supplied the verse 〈qui miseros homines cogens scelus omne patrare〉, thereby preserving the transmitted suadet at III.84.

keywords.name: Konrad Müller
paragraphs: Swiss classical philologist (1920–2016), professor at the University of Bern, renowned for his critical editions of Latin authors.
Editor of T. Lucreti Cari de rerum natura libri sex (Zürich 1975), cited in Deufert's apparatus as C. Müller.
At III.84 he proposed the adverb foede in place of the transmitted suadet, comparing (collato) the internal parallel at I.85 (turparunt sanguine foede).

keywords.name: Cippellarius
paragraphs: Italian humanist copyist of the early 16th century, known through the manuscript of Lucretius he wrote himself.

In 1507 he copied codex Y, now in Piacenza, Biblioteca Comunale Passerini-Landi, 33 (Deufert: Placentinus Bibl. comm. Land. 33, a Cippellario a. 1507 exaratus). While transcribing, he did not limit himself to copying but intervened on the text with his own emendations.
At III.84 he was the first to perceive that the transmitted suadet perverts the syntax of the whole period (qui primus vidit suadet orationem pervertere), and proposed the conjecture suauem.

keywords.name: Otto Zwierlein
paragraphs: German classical philologist (born 1939), professor at the University of Bonn, known for his editions of Seneca's tragedies (Oxford 1986) and his studies on interpolations in Latin poetry.

His conjectures on Lucretius are not published in a work of his own: Deufert learned of them in person, discussing them directly with Zwierlein, and reports and examines them in his study M. Deufert, Pseudo-Lukrezisches im Lukrez. Die unechten Verse in Lukrezens “De rerum natura”, Berolini et Novi Eboraci 1996 (hence the formula Zwierlein apud Deufert).
At III.85–86 he once condemned the two lines as spurious (olim damnavit), as discussed in Deufert (1996) 52 sq., following the lead (praeeunte) of Friedrich Bockemüller.

keywords.name: Friedrich Bockemüller
paragraphs: German classical scholar of the 19th century, editor and commentator of Lucretius.
Author of the edition with commentary T. Lucreti Cari de rerum natura libri sex. Redigirt und erklärt von Friedrich Bockemüller, Stadis 1874.
Cited in the apparatus at III.85–86 as the forerunner (praeeunte Bockemüller) of the athetesis later argued by Otto Zwierlein, since he regarded the two lines as a non-Lucretian interpolation.

keywords.name: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
paragraphs: Early Christian author, rhetorician, and apologist (ca. 250 – ca. 325 AD); preserves crucial indirect quotations from Lucretius in his Divinae Institutiones.
His testimony is valuable because it may reflect textual forms earlier than the medieval manuscript tradition.

keywords.name: Nonius Marcellus
paragraphs: Roman grammarian and lexicographer from Thubursicu (active early 4th century AD); quotes numerous poetic lines in De compendiosa doctrina.
Some Lucretian fragments transmitted by Nonius differ from the medieval manuscripts, offering alternative readings.

keywords.name: Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius
paragraphs: Late antique Roman provincial writer and Neoplatonist philosopher (fl. ca. 400 AD), best known for his encyclopedic dialogue Saturnalia.
His work preserves vital indirect quotations from early Latin poets, including numerous citations from Lucretius illustrating poetic diction and Virgil's models.

Cited in the critical apparatus at III.72 under the siglum Macr. for preserving the correct genitive reading fratris against the erroneous nominative/accusative fratres transmitted by the medieval archetype Ω.

keywords.name: Lucius Annaeus Seneca
paragraphs: Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist and statesman (ca. 4 BC – AD 65), tutor and adviser of Nero.
In his Epistulae morales ad Lucilium (110, 6) he quotes Lucretius' simile of the children who tremble in the dark (III.87–88 = II.55–56).
Cited in the critical apparatus at III.88 under the siglum Sen. for the synonymous variant ita in place of the transmitted sic (cf. the same variation at II.56).
